subject: Biology
description: Transpiration, translocation, plant hormones, photoperiodism, common deficiencies

questions.stem: The loss of water in vapour form from aerial parts of a plant (mainly through stomata) is called:
questions.explanation: Transpiration — ~90% via stomata (microscopic leaf pores), small amounts via cuticle (cuticular) and lenticels. Pulls water up the xylem (transpiration pull / cohesion-tension theory). Cooling effect on the leaf — comparable to sweating. Guttation = loss of LIQUID water from leaf-margin hydathodes when root pressure is high (early-morning droplets on grass). Respiration releases CO₂ + H₂O (gaseous). Translocation = movement of food (mostly sucrose) through phloem.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Auxin — the first plant hormone discovered — is responsible for:
questions.explanation: Auxin (IAA — indole-3-acetic acid) — discovered by Frits Went (1928, Avena coleoptile experiment); building on Charles & Francis Darwin's 1880 phototropism observations. Functions: cell elongation (promotes growth), phototropism (bending toward light), apical dominance (suppresses lateral bud growth — pinch the apex to bush out the plant), parthenocarpy (seedless fruits), root initiation in cuttings. Synthetic auxins — IBA, NAA, 2,4-D (used as a herbicide on broadleaf weeds).
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Which plant hormone induces fruit RIPENING and is a gas at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Ethylene — only gaseous plant hormone. Promotes fruit ripening (mango, banana, tomato, apple), leaf senescence, abscission, breaks dormancy in some seeds. Used commercially in ripening chambers (sealed warehouses with ethylene gas) — replaced calcium carbide (which was banned for releasing acetylene + arsenic-phosphorus impurities). 'One bad apple spoils the bunch' is literal — a damaged apple emits ethylene and accelerates ripening of neighbours. Gibberellins promote stem elongation; cytokinins promote cell division; ABA causes stomatal closure during drought.

questions.stem: Translocation of food (sucrose) in plants takes place through:
questions.explanation: Two transport tissues — Xylem (mostly UPWARD, water + minerals; dead at maturity, hollow) and Phloem (BIDIRECTIONAL, food (sucrose, amino acids); living sieve tubes + companion cells). Translocation explained by Münch's mass-flow / pressure-flow hypothesis (1930) — sucrose loaded at source (leaf) creates osmotic gradient, water enters → high pressure pushes sap to sink (root, fruit, growing tip). Aphids tap into phloem to feed.

questions.stem: The opening and closing of stomata is primarily regulated by:

options.option_text: Abscisic acid (ABA) — closes stomata under stress

questions.explanation: ABA — synthesised in leaves under water stress; signals guard cells to lose K⁺ and water → guard cells become flaccid → stomata close → reduces transpiration. Light + low CO₂ + high humidity → stomata open (guard cells take up K⁺ + water, become turgid). 'Stress hormone' role of ABA also includes seed dormancy maintenance and bud dormancy in winter. The K⁺-pump model is now understood with the proton pump (H⁺-ATPase) being the primary mechanism behind guard-cell turgor.

questions.stem: Plants that flower only when day length is shorter than a critical value are called:

options.option_text: Short-day plants (e.g., chrysanthemum, soybean, rice, cotton)

questions.explanation: Photoperiodism — discovered by Garner & Allard (1920). Categories: SDP (chrysanthemum, soybean, rice, cotton, tobacco — flower in autumn/winter); LDP (wheat, barley, spinach, radish — flower in summer); DNP (tomato, cotton, sunflower — independent of day length). Trick: it's actually the LENGTH of CONTINUOUS DARKNESS that matters (not light) — that's why LDP / SDP can be flipped by interrupting darkness with a brief flash of light. Phytochrome is the protein pigment that senses red/far-red light.
questions.subject: Biology

questions.stem: Yellowing of younger leaves first ('chlorosis') typically indicates deficiency of:

options.option_text: Iron (Fe) — immobile element, deficiency shows in young leaves

questions.explanation: Mobile vs immobile nutrients shapes deficiency-symptom location. MOBILE (N, P, K, Mg): plant moves them from old leaves to new growth — old leaves yellow first. IMMOBILE (Ca, Fe, S, B, Mn): can't be retranslocated — young leaves yellow first. Iron deficiency = interveinal chlorosis (veins stay green, leaf blade between yellows) on YOUNG leaves. Common in alkaline / lime soils where Fe gets locked. Cure: chelated iron (Fe-EDTA), foliar sprays.
